title: Choir and Smile
premise: Coral Pemberton, a rationalist property surveyor, is hired to appraise her late grandmother's house and discovers that every photograph taken inside now contains a thirteenth chair — a chair that appears in the room itself when no one is looking. The house was built over a dry well where, generations ago, the Pemberton family choir sang a hymn to keep something down; the song has eleven verses, and the last verse was never written down. As Coral's skepticism erodes, she must recover the final verse from the memories of the house's previous singers — including her grandmother's ghost, who traded her voice for Coral's survival decades ago. In the climax, Coral learns the last verse but refuses to sing it, instead giving the house what it truly wanted: an audience, not a chorus, breaking the pact of complicity that fed it. The well refills with silence, the chair vanishes from every photograph, and Coral inherits the house — empty at last, though she keeps one photo with the chair in it, as a promise never to forget.
about_author: C. M. Lockridge is the pen name of a former church organist turned land surveyor who spent fifteen years cataloguing condemned properties across rural England. They write horror about buildings that remember, insisting their fiction is entirely invented while declining to say which houses they have refused to enter twice.

chapters.title: The Thirteenth Chair
chapters.summary: POV Coral. A property surveyor with a reputation for debunking 'haunted' listings takes the job appraising her estranged grandmother's estate, finding the paperwork oddly urgent. In every photograph of the interior — old and new alike — there is an extra wooden chair pulled up to the table. Coral counts twelve chairs in the room. Emotional beat: professional confidence masking old family guilt.

chapters.title: Probate and Cold Rooms
chapters.summary: POV Coral. Coral spends her first night in the house to meet a contractual deadline, cataloguing rooms that measure differently on each pass. The heating works everywhere except the hallway, where her breath fogs in July. She finds grandmother Edith's surveyor's license — identical number to Coral's own. Emotional beat: uncanny familiarity, the sense of walking a path already walked.

chapters.title: What the Neighbors Won't Say
chapters.summary: POV Coral. In the village pub, Coral probes locals about the house; conversations die mid-sentence when she mentions the well or the name Pemberton. An elderly man, Mr. Aldous, presses a hymnal into her hands and says only: 'Eleven verses. Never ask for twelve.' Emotional beat: isolation sharpening into dread.

chapters.title: The Chair Moves Closer
chapters.summary: POV Coral. Reviewing her own appraisal photos that night, Coral finds the extra chair now positioned nearer the camera in each successive shot — a sequence, like something approaching. She photographs the dining room deliberately; the chair appears facing her. Emotional beat: the skeptic's toolkit turning against her, evidence accumulating despite herself.

chapters.title: Edith's Tape Recorder
chapters.summary: POV Coral. In the attic Coral finds reel-to-reel tapes labeled by year, recordings of Edith singing alone — a hymn Coral half-remembers from childhood. On the 1974 tape, a second voice joins uninvited, and Edith stops mid-verse, whispering 'not yet, not the last.' Emotional beat: grief complicated by fear of what her grandmother knew.

chapters.title: Aldous Explains Nothing
chapters.summary: POV Coral and Aldous (alternating). Aldous reveals he was the choir's accompanist: nine singers, one song, one well kept quiet since 1893. Every generation renews the singing; Edith was the last voice, and her death has started a countdown. He refuses to say what happens when the well refills. Emotional beat: reluctant alliance, duty inherited like debt.

chapters.title: Verse Ten
chapters.summary: POV Coral. Following the hymnal's marginalia, Coral descends to the cellar and finds the well mouth beneath a false floor — dry, deep, breathing warmth. Standing there, she involuntarily hums verse ten and hears it answered from below, note-perfect, a half-second behind. Emotional beat: the first undeniable proof, and the horror of having participated.

chapters.title: The Photographs Begin Moving
chapters.summary: POV Coral. The chair in the photos is now occupied — a blurred figure, then less blurred each day. Coral recognizes the posture: Edith. Her grandmother's image sits in the thirteenth chair in every picture ever taken in the house, including Coral's own childhood snapshots. Emotional beat: love weaponized; the dead reaching through memory.

chapters.title: Nine Voices, Eight Graves
chapters.summary: POV Aldous. Flashback chapter: 1968, the choir's renewal ceremony gone wrong when one singer tried to stop singing mid-verse. What the well took, and what it left. Aldous has spent fifty years unable to enter the house. Emotional beat: survivor's guilt as exposition; the cost of the pact made flesh.

chapters.title: Duty Calls Collect
chapters.summary: POV Coral. Coral's firm demands the completed appraisal; her career, her flat deposit, her whole rational life hang on signing off a house she now knows is a mouth. She drafts the report calling it structurally sound and cannot submit it. Emotional beat: power and its corruption — the institution needs her lie more than her truth.

chapters.title: The Verse That Isn't There
chapters.summary: POV Coral. Coral searches for the eleventh verse — the last before the unwritten twelfth — in parish records, Edith's papers, the hymnal's gutters. She finds a page torn out and, pressed in Edith's Bible, a single line of notation and the words: 'the rest you must be told.' Emotional beat: hope curdling into the realization that knowledge here is transmitted, not recorded.

chapters.title: Séance by Reel-to-Reel
chapters.summary: POV Coral. Playing all the tapes simultaneously in the dining room, Coral attempts contact. The thirteenth chair scrapes into position behind her; Edith's recorded voice deviates from the recording, addressing Coral directly: 'Don't learn it from me. I paid too much for my version.' Emotional beat: tenderness inside terror; the ghost protecting, not haunting.

chapters.title: The House Appraises Back
chapters.summary: POV Coral. The house begins evaluating Coral: doors open onto rooms from her childhood, her debts itemized in dust on the hall table, her loneliness measured in cold spots shaped like arms. It offers her a place — the twelfth singer's seat, vacant since 1968. Emotional beat: temptation; the corruption of being wanted by something powerful.

chapters.title: Aldous Returns
chapters.summary: POV Aldous. Breaking his fifty-year vow, Aldous enters the house to stop Coral descending again. He confesses the full mechanics: the well refills when the song falls silent for a full turn of seasons; the last verse sung aloud completes the contract and binds the singer forever. Emotional beat: an old man spending his last courage on a stranger's granddaughter.

chapters.title: What Edith Traded
chapters.summary: POV Edith (ghost, 1999 flashback). Edith, dying, negotiated with the house: her voice in exchange for the well staying quiet long enough for Coral — the granddaughter she'd never met — to grow up free. The house agreed, and has been patient. Emotional beat: love against duty; a grandmother's bargain revealed as the story's hidden engine.

chapters.title: The Countdown Audible
chapters.summary: POV Coral. Winter arrives early inside the house. The well can be heard filling — water sounds rising through the floors, the hymn humming itself in the walls, missing only a lead voice. Coral realizes the house doesn't need her consent anymore, just her breath near an open mouth. Emotional beat: ticking clock made literal; agency shrinking.

chapters.title: Learning the Last Verse
chapters.summary: POV Coral. From Edith's Bible line, Aldous's memory, and the tapes played backward, Coral reconstructs the final verse — and discovers its terrible design: it isn't a plea or a ward, it's a signature. Sung, it makes the singer a co-owner of the well. Emotional beat: comprehension as horror; the trap was always educational.

chapters.title: The Firm Sends a Replacement
chapters.summary: POV Coral and junior surveyor Dev (alternating). Coral's firm sends Dev to finish the appraisal. Coral races back to find him photographing the dining room, the thirteenth chair beside him, already humming a tune he says he 'can't get out of his head.' Emotional beat: guilt and urgency; Coral's delay has endangered someone innocent.

chapters.title: Twelve Chairs, Thirteen Voices
chapters.summary: POV Coral. The house pulls Coral, Dev, and Aldous into the photograph-space — the frozen middle of every picture at once — where the eight dead singers stand in their chairs, waiting for a quorum. The well below is three-quarters full. Emotional beat: climax approach; the past and present occupying a single frame.

chapters.title: The Verse Refused
chapters.summary: POV Coral. At the well's lip, with the melody pulling at her lungs, Coral understands the house's true hunger: not a singer but a believer, someone to make the pact real again. She stands before the thirteenth chair and does the one thing no Pemberton has done — listens to the whole song without joining, witnessing it, refusing complicity. The house convulses. Emotional beat: the climax; silence as defiance, attention without participation.

chapters.title: Refill
chapters.summary: POV Coral. Unwitnessed belief cannot hold; the pact voids. The well fills — with clean water, then stillness — and the dead singers bow out of their chairs like a choir dismissed. Edith's image lingers longest, mouths 'clever girl,' and fades. Dev and Aldous wake on the lawn; the house stands ordinary, measurable, cold in the honest way. Emotional beat: exhaustion after rupture; survival at a price — Coral heard every verse and will carry them.

chapters.title: Sold, With One Exception
chapters.summary: POV Coral. Coral files the appraisal truthfully and buys the house herself with her savings, keeping it empty. She hangs one photograph — the childhood snapshot with the thirteenth chair — in the hall as a covenant of memory. On quiet evenings she hums nothing at all, and the house, listening, stays silent too. Emotional beat: resolution; love without duty, survival without forgetting.
